items.claim: Prior work has looked at personal political orientation and regional political climate separately as predictors of COVID-19 vaccine attitudes. Few studies have examined how the two interact.
The study asks whether regional political climate moderates the link between individual political orientation and COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake.
The interaction did not hold for initial vaccine status. The authors attribute this gap between attitudes and action to widespread vaccine mandates.
The mechanism behind the interaction, such as social pressure, was not assessed.

Cowan, Mark and Reich [18] argued that political orientation has become a better predictor of vaccine hesitancy than demographics, fear or institutional trust. The authors build on this by extending the influence of orientation to the surrounding climate.

The paper asks how partisan polarization in online COVID-19 discourse varied across subnational regions and over time in the United States and Canada. To answer this, it develops a new computational way to measure that variation.
After filtering for COVID-19 content, the dataset contains about 12.5 million U.S. tweets and 46.6 million Canadian tweets.

The tweets come from late 2020 while the vaccination data come from 2021, so the vaccine correlations are suggestive rather than causal. More generally, the paper's correlations do not establish causation.

The authors extend prior research on partisan COVID-19 responses. They agree with its finding that right-leaning regions were more divided, then go further by characterizing geographic heterogeneity and change over time.
They qualify Merkley et al.'s [103] finding of a cross-partisan consensus among Canadians on emergency measures, arguing that this consensus did not carry over to social media.

In the U.S., polarization in vaccine discourse is strongly and negatively linked to vaccination rates, which the authors read as a sign of real public health consequences. This link is much weaker in Canada.

In the U.S., Republican vote share is significantly correlated with polarization on masks and vaccines but not on lockdowns. In Canada, the corresponding associations are not statistically significant.
Party labels rely on self-reported information, and Bloc Québécois supporters were excluded.
They build on earlier studies [10,62], Allcott et al. and Morris, which found that conservative states showed higher polarization in response to public health interventions.
The authors contrast their Canadian conspiracy result with Owen et al. [94], who reported less negative sentiment in Canadian vaccine-related tweets during 2020.

The study asks how the Democratic Party's spread of stigmatizing labels for Trump affected Democrats' perceptions of people with criminal records, and how it affected Democrats' sense of being represented by their own elected officials.
The study also asks whether a counterexample can offset the advertisement's negative effects. The counterexample is the perspective of a formerly system-involved representative on the label.
The paper argues against the Democratic Party's use of stigmatizing terms. It accepts that acknowledging Trump's convictions was necessary.
Seeing the 'convicted criminal' Trump advertisement worsened Democrats' perceptions of people with criminal records but improved their perceived representation.
A counter-stereotype narrative shown before the advertisement largely undid its negative effect on perceptions of people with records.
The counter-narrative was a lightly edited news excerpt in which a formerly incarcerated Nevada assemblymember gives his perspective.
In supplemental analyses, the advertisement was more damaging to perceptions of people with records among system-impacted respondents.
The study offers only preliminary evidence.
The effect of the mugshot image cannot be separated from the effect of the stigmatizing label.
Social desirability bias or a Hawthorne effect cannot be ruled out.
The study cannot rule out that the intervention creates a new category of deservingness rather than reducing stigma.
The study extends social categorization theory to political advertising. It argues that labeling a salient exemplar (Trump) spills over onto perceptions of the whole group of people with records.
The study draws on Prospect Theory to interpret the representation effects, with Trump serving as a reference point.
The paper qualifies the literature on generative AI threats to online surveys (e.g., Westwood), noting that it mostly concerns open-text responses.
YouGov panelists were linked to their X handles (2,567 linked users), and about 9.25 million of their public posts were scraped between March 2019 and January 2021.

Prior work (Petersen, Osmundsen and Arceneaux; Bail) links hostility to deprivation, marginalization or personality. The authors argue hostility is also tied to political engagement.
Hebbelstrup Rye Rasmussen and Petersen found that hostility and partisan extremity are bidirectionally related. The authors cite this to support the possibility of reciprocal influences.

The paper asks whether the selection and influence links between substance use and friendship, found in diverse schools, also hold where students are predominantly AI and kinship and community norms may orient relationships differently.

Friendship ties among AI adolescents in reservation schools are driven mainly by universal structural mechanisms (reciprocity, transitivity) and by demographic homophily (gender, grade, sexual orientation), not by substance use.

Substance use had no consistent sender, receiver or homophily effects. The few isolated effects (alcohol homophily in School B, an alcohol sender effect in School C) did not replicate across schools or substances.

Network processes varied with institutional context. Only the private preparatory school (School C) showed a centralized popularity hierarchy, which the authors read as egalitarian norms operating in the tribal schools.

The authors place the study within adolescent social network research built mostly on heterogeneous schools. They aim to revise its generalizations by studying a setting where AI youth are the majority.

They combine standard endogenous network mechanisms with a cultural view in which tie-formation mechanisms are not culturally neutral. Their conclusion revises the framework: the structural processes are universal, but their parameters are calibrated by context.

Non-AI intervention researchers (e.g., Hunter et al.'s review) have used the substance use–friendship link as the basis for network interventions. The authors question whether such interventions would be effective for AI youth.
